summary: Suggests a file format that tells mail reading programs which locally installed tools can handle which kinds of multimedia mail, so several programs can share one configuration.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1524 proposes a shared configuration file that mail programs can consult when they receive a media type they cannot handle directly. Each entry names a type and a command, with optional rules that control when and how the command runs.

subtitle: A shared file format for telling mail programs which local tools handle each media type.

tldr.problem: Mail programs need a common way to learn which locally installed tools can display, compose, edit or print different media types.
tldr.mechanism: A mailcap file maps a content type to a viewing command and may include optional commands, flags and tests; user agents search configured files for a matching entry.
tldr.outcome: The memo proposes an operating-system-independent format with UNIX behavior in an appendix and warns that automatic command execution needs care.

today: RFC 1524 is an Informational memo published in September 1993, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It proposes a mailcap format and gives UNIX-specific behavior in an appendix.

sections.title: Why Mail Programs Need a Shared File
sections.content:
RFC 1524 addresses the shift from text-only mail to messages containing multiple media types. The memo says different mail user agents often could not exchange non-text content unless they had been designed to work together.

It proposes that a user agent consult an external configuration file when it encounters an unfamiliar type. If user agents share a common format and source for this information, a site can add support by installing a program and adding an entry to the file.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail program can use a configuration file to find a local tool for unfamiliar content. This lets different mail programs use the same type-to-command information.

sections.title: Finding a Matching Entry
sections.content:
A user agent reads mailcap information from a designated set of files, treated as if combined. Users can add to or override site settings. The agent uses the first matching entry that has the needed information and whose optional test succeeds.

The file contains entries separated by newlines. Blank lines and lines beginning with a hash character are ignored, and an entry can continue onto another line when a line ends with a backslash. The exact file locations depend on the operating system; the memo specifies a default search path for UNIX and allows the MAILCAPS environment variable to override it.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail program searches configured files and uses the first entry that fits and passes its test. Users can supply settings that add to or override the site's settings.

sections.title: Fields in a Mailcap Entry
sections.content:
Each entry has semicolon-separated fields. The first field identifies a content type, matched against the message's Content-Type header; an asterisk subtype matches all subtypes. The required second field gives the command used to view the content.

Optional fields can name commands for composing, editing or printing, or a test that decides whether the entry applies. Flags can indicate that a command needs an interactive terminal or produces output that should be scrollable. The format also provides fields for descriptions, filename templates and local extensions beginning with x-.
sections.plainLanguage: The first two fields say what kind of content the entry handles and which command displays it. Optional fields describe other commands or conditions for using the entry.

sections.title: Command Substitutions on UNIX
sections.content:
The UNIX appendix defines commands as full command lines intended for the Bourne shell. In a command, %s can stand for a file containing the message body, and %t can stand for its content type and subtype. A parameter from a Content-Type field can be included with the %{name} form.

The appendix also defines substitutions for multipart content: %n gives the number of sub-parts, and %F gives content types and file names for the parts. A test command returns zero when its condition is true and a non-zero code otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: On UNIX, special markers in a command are replaced with information about the message before the program runs. For example, %s can be replaced with the name of a file holding the content.

sections.title: Caution with Automatically Run Programs
sections.content: The memo does not discuss security in detail, but warns that the mechanism can make it easier for implementations to encounter security problems described in the MIME document. A mailcap file can cause programs to run on received content, so the memo specifically advises implementors and administrators to be careful about which programs they list for automatic execution.
sections.plainLanguage: A mailcap entry can cause a program to run on received content. Administrators should choose carefully which commands are allowed to run automatically.

data.title: Sample mailcap entries

text/richtext; richtext %s; copiousoutput
audio/*; showaudio; test=/usr/local/bin/hasaudio
